label: the two load-bearing C-only concepts — kc-order-numbers and statistical-question

widget.prompt: Counting goes 4, 5, ?, 7. Slide the marker to where the missing number lives on the line.

commonPlacements.feedback: 8 sits AFTER 7, but the missing number comes before it — it belongs in the gap between 5 and 7.
5 is already there, just before the gap. The missing number is the very next one.
3 comes before 4, so it is behind where the counting has already reached. The gap is between 5 and 7.

widget.successFeedback: 6 — and the line shows why it could not be anything else: it is the one spot with 5 on its left and 7 on its right. Counting order is a position on the line, not a fact to recall.
widget.lowFeedback: Too far left — the marker is below 5, but the missing number comes after 5.
widget.highFeedback: Too far right — the marker is past 7, but the missing number comes before 7.

widget.prompt: Eleven students answered "How many minutes did you spend on homework last night?" Build their answers: 1 said 10, 3 said 20, 4 said 30, 2 said 40, 1 said 50.
widget.successFeedback: Look at what you just built — the answers SPREAD out. That spread is exactly what makes the question statistical: it anticipates variety. Ask instead "how many minutes are in an hour?" and every dot would stack on 60 in one tower, because that question has only one answer.
widget.partialFeedback: Some stacks are the wrong height. Recount from the data: 1 at 10, 3 at 20, 4 at 30, 2 at 40, 1 at 50.
